# Swarm

On Codex, read the [platform mapping](../poteto-mode/references/codex-tools.md), including its per-skill notes, before following this skill.

On GitHub Copilot, read the [platform mapping](../poteto-mode/references/copilot-tools.md), including its per-skill notes, before following this skill.

## Start

Open a todolist with one entry per phase before launching anything.

1. Frame
2. Fan out
3. Aggregate
4. Report

## Phase A: Frame

1. State the done predicate and the artifact or report the swarm must return.
2. Choose the shape. Partition into slices, race N workers on identical briefs, or mix both. For a race or mixed shape, declare `first pass`, `rank all`, or `best-of` before spawning.
4. Pick the worker model from the `swarm workers` line in `pstack-models.md`. If the sheet or that line is missing, use the default in [Models](#models). For `auto` or `inherit-parent`, omit `model` so the workers run on the parent model. If the `Agent` tool rejects a slug, use the default and say so. If it rejects the default, use the closest valid slug of the same family from its error message. For a model race, name each arm's model up front. Pick each subagent's reasoning level for the job, per the Subagents section of the **poteto-mode** skill.
5. Give each worker its own writable output when it writes. When workers verify or measure commits, each brief names the exact SHAs. A measurement brief also names the method (sample count, what one sample is, order). The worker records both in its result.

## Phase B: Fan out

Spawn all N workers in one message with `subagent_type: "general-purpose"`, `run_in_background: true`, and the step 4 model, left unset for `auto` or `inherit-parent`. Claude Code subagents all run on this machine, so isolation comes from the worktree or output directory assigned in Phase A, not from a remote environment.

When a worker must start from a non-default branch, check that branch out in the worker's own worktree and name the worktree path in its brief.

Every brief stands alone. Include the goal, scope, exact slice or race arm, how to verify, and what to report. Reports use `PASS`, `ISSUES`, or `BLOCKED` with evidence. A worker that can prove a defect reports `ISSUES` and lists every issue it can prove, not only the first.

If a worker drops out, proceed with N-1 and note it.

## Phase C: Aggregate

Read the terminal results. Drop a result that does not record the SHAs and method its brief names, and respawn that worker once. After a second miss, record a gap. A gap does not count as a pass. For coverage, every required slice needs a result. For a race, apply the selection rule declared up front. Use first pass, rank all, or best-of. Do not paste raw worker dumps.

## Phase D: Report

Return one consolidated in-chat report with the table, issue one-liners, gaps or dropouts, and the race rule when used.

## Models

Role defaults, stamped from `plugins/pstack/models.json` (edit there, rerun `tools/generate.mjs`). A matching role line in the `pstack-models.md` override sheet overrides each at runtime; `/setup-pstack` writes it and lists its path per runtime.

- swarm workers: `opus`

## Reasoning effort

A role value in the override sheet may name a reasoning effort after its model, as in `opus @xhigh`. Levels on Claude Code: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`. Which ones apply depends on the model. A value without `@` takes the sheet's `default effort` line, a level or `session`, and `session` when the sheet has no such line. `session` sets no effort, so the dispatch is the usual one. Strip the suffix before reading the model: `inherit-parent` or `auto` still omits `model` at every level, and a model name is passed as `model`. On Claude Code, a level picks the effort agent from the `subagent_type` you would otherwise use. `pstack:poteto-agent` becomes `subagent_type: "pstack:poteto-agent-<level>"`. `general-purpose`, or no `subagent_type`, becomes `subagent_type: "pstack:effort-<level>"`. The effort agents set only `effort`, so the model you pass still decides the model. On Codex, pass the level as `spawn_agent`'s `reasoning_effort` and keep the usual instructions.

# Task: awesome.video improvement waves (analytics onward paths, researcher engine, guided researcher view, full functional audit)

Paste this into Claude Code (or another agent harness) started at the root of a fresh clone of `krzemienski/awesome-list-site`.

## Context and Assumptions
<task_context>
- **Source inputs:**
  * The owner's structured work order for four connected pieces (A to D).
  * Analytics findings from Replit Analytics for Oct 18–24, 2026.
  * Researcher run history.
  * Files read from the repo at commit `5a4e0d8`. Findings are listed below.
- **Background:** awesome.video is a curated catalog of video-engineering resources. It is a TypeScript monorepo:
  * Express server run by `tsx` in `server/`
  * React and Vite client in `client/src/`
  * PostgreSQL through Drizzle in `shared/schema.ts`
  * Clerk sign-in
  * An AI "researcher" in `server/ai/` that finds new resources with the Claude Agent SDK
- **Why this matters:** Search traffic lands on resource pages and leaves. Of 87 Google visits that started on a resource page, only 12 viewed a second page. Only 26 of 213 sessions looked at more than one resource or category. Owner and QA traffic pollutes the numbers. The researcher has not run on the env configuration in production since July. Its last dev run recorded `turns_used = 0` with 3 discoveries and approved nothing.
- **Definition of done:** All four pieces are merged into `main` in dependency order, and each piece's finish lines are shown with browser or curl evidence. `docs/audits/full-functional-audit-<date>.md` records a final full pass with no known failures. One standalone final report is delivered.
- **Urgency:** This is a multi-wave autonomous run. Nobody is watching it live.
- **Scope:** Pieces A to D exactly as specified. Out of scope:
  * new features beyond the fixes D requires
  * production writes, publishing or deploying
  * any test, script, gate or CI tooling

  If a better approach exists, say so in one sentence and continue as asked.

**Pre-read findings (repo at `5a4e0d8`). Confirm each against current code before you rely on it:**
- `client/src/hooks/use-analytics.tsx` imports `onCLS`, `onINP` and `onLCP` from `web-vitals` (^6.2.1). FID comes from a hand-written `PerformanceObserver({ type: 'first-input' })`, and `onFCP` and `onTTFB` are not wired up. The comment on `trackPerformance` in `analytics.ts` still mentions FID.
- `client/src/lib/analytics.ts`:
  * Every event goes through the module-private `track()`, which lazy-loads `analytics-dispatch.ts`. `trackPageView` also goes through `track()`, with `replit: false`.
  * `CommandPaletteOpenMethod` is `'keyboard_shortcut' | 'slash_key' | 'header_button'`.
  * `trackRelatedResourceOpened` and `trackRelatedCategoryOpened` have no `surface` property today. `trackTagInteraction` already has one.
- `server/ai/anthropicConfig.ts` is the shared resolver. Credential precedence is router (BASE_URL + AUTH_TOKEN) → router (BASE_URL + API_KEY) → managed → direct → none. It fails closed when BASE_URL is set without a credential. A missing `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_<TIER>_MODEL` silently falls back to `FIRST_PARTY_TIER_MODELS` (for example `claude-sonnet-4-5`). Subagents receive the tier alias, and the CLI maps it through the same env variables. `describeAnthropicConfig()` already gives a secret-free snapshot.
- `package.json`: `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` ^0.3.272, `@anthropic-ai/sdk` ^0.125.0, `zod` ^4.4.3, `framer-motion` ^11.18.2. Scripts: `dev`, `type-check` (`tsc --noEmit`), `lint`.
- Project memory relevant to these pieces (topic files under `.agents/memory/`). Read each one when you reach its area:
  * Analytics: `analytics-browser-verification.md`, `analytics-shared-sender.md`, `umami-spa-pageviews-history-restore.md` (Replit SPA pageviews fixed Oct 24; can only be confirmed after publishing), `click-time-auth-gates.md` (`isAuthenticated` is provisionally false while Clerk loads lazily), `pageview-loading-titles.md`, `hidden-fallback-cls.md`, `lcp-and-prepaint.md`, `tags-metadata-source.md` (real tags live in `resources.metadata.tags`; the tags table is empty).
  * Researcher: `agent-sdk-migration.md`, `aborted-agent-run-usage.md`, `sdk-block-split-messages.md` (one API turn spans several assistant messages sharing a `message.id`; dedupe by id), `sdk-tool-schema-leniency.md`, `anthropic-midloop-steering.md`, `ai-job-liveness.md` (USD-cap stops use status `budget_stopped`), `llm-json-output-hygiene.md`.
  * Environment: `dev-server-no-watch.md`, `dev-listener-selection.md` (address port 5000 explicitly), `vite-workspace-watch-reload.md`, `before-fix-proof-instance.md` (a second dev instance must not share `node_modules/.vite`, or React loads twice), `parallel-subagent-file-clobber.md`, `platform-git-autocommit.md`, `workspace-recycles.md`.
  * Audit: `tester-finding-retractions.md`, `audit-cold-boot-flake.md`, `qa-report-stale-schema.md`, `qa-throwaway-user-teardown.md`, `jit-teardown-order.md`, `catalog-http-cache-vs-invalidation.md`, `headless-e2e-gotchas.md` (dismiss the consent banner first), `radix-interaction-pitfalls.md`, `cmdk-live-region-placement.md`, `resource-status-public-gate.md`.

**Assumptions made (high impact first):**
- Assumed: admin suppression must also cover events that fire before Clerk finishes loading. Use a marker that can be read synchronously, set on admin sign-in and cleared on sign-out (or an equivalent that you justify), and check it inside the shared sender. Basis: Clerk loads lazily, and `isAuthenticated` is provisionally false (`click-time-auth-gates.md`). Impact if wrong: high, because admin landing pageviews would leak.
- Assumed: `/admin` and `/bookmarks` pollution is removed by suppressing admin sessions, not by blocking paths. `/bookmarks` stays tracked for real visitors. The QA path list is the `/qa-*` prefix plus sentinel ids such as `/resource/999999999`. Basis: "Real visitors are tracked exactly as before." Impact if wrong: high.
- Assumed: the strict "no silent fallback" preflight applies to the researcher launch path. It requires `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` + `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`, and the scout tier variable to be set explicitly. The shared resolver's behaviour for other flows stays unchanged. Basis: the tier fallback to `FIRST_PARTY_TIER_MODELS` in `anthropicConfig.ts`, plus the requirement that enrichment and other calls keep using the shared resolver. Impact if wrong: medium.
- Assumed: "a different agent from the author reviews each piece" is met by making subagents the authors of all code changes (A, B, C and D's fix groups). The main agent is reviewer and final browser verifier. No extra verifier subagents are created. Impact if wrong: medium.
- Assumed: server-emitted conversions from agent test sign-ups (for example Mixpanel `sign_up_completed` from Clerk JIT) are outside the shared client sender. Report them as a follow-up for D or the owner. Impact if wrong: medium.
- Assumed: the resource-page and listing-page search entry opens the existing command palette and emits `command_palette_opened` with a new `open_method` (for example `resource_page_button`). The palette's existing route to `/search` covers full results. Impact if wrong: medium.
- Assumed: git worktrees work in this local clone. `before-fix-proof-instance.md` records that `git worktree add` is blocked only in Replit's shell. If worktrees are blocked here, run A and then B on separate branches in the main checkout. Impact if wrong: low.
- Assumed: each worktree gets its own `npm install`, and its own port if `server/index.ts` honours a port variable. If the port is hard-coded, verify A and B one at a time on port 5000 rather than changing the port logic. Impact if wrong: low.
- Assumed: "browser tools" means the harness's interactive browser tools (for example a browser MCP server from `.mcp.json`). Driving them call by call is allowed. Writing harness scripts is not. Impact if wrong: low.
- Assumed: the target SDK versions are read from npm at run time. At writing time, 0.3.310 and 1.3.0 were current. Impact if wrong: low.
</task_context>

## Hard Rules (from the owner; quoted text is verbatim)
<hard_rules>
- "Verification: never write or execute scripts (Playwright/Node/shell harnesses). Drive the real app through the in-app browser / browser tools directly."
- Never create, register or run validation scripts, test suites, drift, pixel or performance gates, CI test jobs, proof packets or reviewer panels. They were deleted on purpose.
- Verify by driving the running app in a real browser at three widths:
  * desktop (1440×900)
  * tablet (820×1180)
  * phone (390×844)

  Use single `curl` requests for API reads. `npm run type-check` and `npm run lint` are allowed and must stay clean for the files you touch.
- Use no mocks, stubs, fake data, test-mode bypasses or silent fallbacks. If the real system does not work, fix the real system.
- Production is read-only. Do not publish or deploy. When something can only be confirmed on the published site, finish everything else and list it as an owner step: "publish, then check X".
- Never rename a live analytics event, because dashboards depend on the names. The event catalog in `docs/ANALYTICS.md` decides names. Every custom event goes through the module-private `track()` in `client/src/lib/analytics.ts` via a typed helper.
- Public resources have status `approved`. Journeys have status `published`.
- Do not add any test files or scripts, permanent or scratch.
</hard_rules>

## Agent Behavior
<agent_behavior>
<default_to_action>
Implement changes rather than only suggesting them. When intent is unclear, infer the most useful likely action and use tools to find missing details instead of guessing. You are operating autonomously, and the owner cannot answer mid-task. For reversible actions that follow from this work order, proceed without asking. Stop only for destructive actions, production writes, or real scope changes.
</default_to_action>

<investigate_before_answering>
Read a file before you make claims about it or edit it. Re-read it right before editing, because subagents and merges change files under you. When you change a symbol, search every reference: calls, types, string literals, dynamic imports, re-exports, config and docs. Trust current code over a memory file that disagrees, and update that memory file when it does.
</investigate_before_answering>

<use_parallel_tool_calls>
Make independent tool calls and file reads in parallel. Serialize only calls whose inputs depend on earlier results. Never use placeholders or guessed parameters.
</use_parallel_tool_calls>

<scope_fidelity>
Deliver what was asked, at the scope intended. In pieces A, B and C, leave pre-existing bugs, performance concerns and unmentioned behaviour alone unless the requested behaviour cannot work without the fix. Log each one as a follow-up; piece D picks them up. Where a piece is ambiguous, implement the reading that its wording and the surrounding code most directly support, and record that assumption. Do not build for other readings. Keep edits surgical: change the lines that need changing rather than rewriting whole files.
</scope_fidelity>

<subagent_delegation>
Subagents are the authors of code changes, and the main agent orchestrates, reviews and verifies. The owner requires that a different agent from the author reviews each piece. Give each subagent a self-contained brief containing:
- the goal and the files
- every hard rule above, verbatim
- the relevant memory topic files
- what done means
- how to verify it in the browser

Treat a subagent's report as claims. Read its diff, check its evidence, and do the final browser verification yourself. Shared files are contested: the state file, `.agents/memory/MEMORY.md`, and any doc touched by more than one piece. The main agent edits those, and only after the subagents touching them have finished (`parallel-subagent-file-clobber.md`).
</subagent_delegation>

<progress_updates>
Before your first tool call, say in one sentence what you are about to do. While working, give a brief update only on important findings, wave transitions or changes of direction. The final report leads with the outcome.
</progress_updates>

<persistence>
Your context may be compacted during this long run. Do not stop early because of token budget. Keep `.local/state/improvement-waves.md` current with decisions, progress per piece, branch names and what is left, so that a fresh context can resume. If the last thing you wrote is a plan, a list of next steps or a promise about work you have not done, do that work now with tool calls. End only when every finish line is met, or when you are blocked on input only the owner can give. In that case, report what you tried and exactly what you need.
</persistence>

<state_changes>
Before a command that changes system state (restarts, deletes, config edits, database writes), confirm that the evidence supports that specific action. A signal that looks like a known failure may have a different cause. Any repo write reloads every open Vite page, so finish a browser check before you edit files.
</state_changes>
</agent_behavior>

  * more like this
  * the rest of the category
  * tags that lead to existing tag pages, derived from `resources.metadata.tags`

# Swarm

On Codex, read the [platform mapping](../poteto-mode/references/codex-tools.md), including its per-skill notes, before following this skill.

On GitHub Copilot, read the [platform mapping](../poteto-mode/references/copilot-tools.md), including its per-skill notes, before following this skill.

## Start

Open a todolist with one entry per phase before launching anything.

1. Frame
2. Fan out
3. Aggregate
4. Report

## Phase A: Frame

1. State the done predicate and the artifact or report the swarm must return.
2. Choose the shape. Partition into slices, race N workers on identical briefs, or mix both. For a race or mixed shape, declare `first pass`, `rank all`, or `best-of` before spawning.
4. Pick the worker model from the `swarm workers` line in `pstack-models.md`. If the sheet or that line is missing, use the default in [Models](#models). For `auto` or `inherit-parent`, omit `model` so the workers run on the parent model. If the `Agent` tool rejects a slug, use the default and say so. If it rejects the default, use the closest valid slug of the same family from its error message. For a model race, name each arm's model up front. Pick each subagent's reasoning level for the job, per the Subagents section of the **poteto-mode** skill.
5. Give each worker its own writable output when it writes. When workers verify or measure commits, each brief names the exact SHAs. A measurement brief also names the method (sample count, what one sample is, order). The worker records both in its result.

## Phase B: Fan out

Spawn all N workers in one message with `subagent_type: "general-purpose"`, `run_in_background: true`, and the step 4 model, left unset for `auto` or `inherit-parent`. Claude Code subagents all run on this machine, so isolation comes from the worktree or output directory assigned in Phase A, not from a remote environment.

When a worker must start from a non-default branch, check that branch out in the worker's own worktree and name the worktree path in its brief.

Every brief stands alone. Include the goal, scope, exact slice or race arm, how to verify, and what to report. Reports use `PASS`, `ISSUES`, or `BLOCKED` with evidence. A worker that can prove a defect reports `ISSUES` and lists every issue it can prove, not only the first.

If a worker drops out, proceed with N-1 and note it.

## Phase C: Aggregate

Read the terminal results. Drop a result that does not record the SHAs and method its brief names, and respawn that worker once. After a second miss, record a gap. A gap does not count as a pass. For coverage, every required slice needs a result. For a race, apply the selection rule declared up front. Use first pass, rank all, or best-of. Do not paste raw worker dumps.

## Phase D: Report

Return one consolidated in-chat report with the table, issue one-liners, gaps or dropouts, and the race rule when used.

## Models

Role defaults, stamped from `plugins/pstack/models.json` (edit there, rerun `tools/generate.mjs`). A matching role line in the `pstack-models.md` override sheet overrides each at runtime; `/setup-pstack` writes it and lists its path per runtime.

- swarm workers: `opus`

## Reasoning effort

A role value in the override sheet may name a reasoning effort after its model, as in `opus @xhigh`. Levels on Claude Code: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`. Which ones apply depends on the model. A value without `@` takes the sheet's `default effort` line, a level or `session`, and `session` when the sheet has no such line. `session` sets no effort, so the dispatch is the usual one. Strip the suffix before reading the model: `inherit-parent` or `auto` still omits `model` at every level, and a model name is passed as `model`. On Claude Code, a level picks the effort agent from the `subagent_type` you would otherwise use. `pstack:poteto-agent` becomes `subagent_type: "pstack:poteto-agent-<level>"`. `general-purpose`, or no `subagent_type`, becomes `subagent_type: "pstack:effort-<level>"`. The effort agents set only `effort`, so the model you pass still decides the model. On Codex, pass the level as `spawn_agent`'s `reasoning_effort` and keep the usual instructions.

## Principles

Read the leaf skill in full for any principle you apply. Each entry names when it applies. Each leaf is the **principle-<title>** skill, with the title in kebab case, hyphens kept and other punctuation dropped, unless the entry gives its name.

**Core**

- **Laziness Protocol.** Refactoring, sizing a diff, or tempted to add abstractions, layers, or signal threading. Bias to deletion and the smallest change that solves the problem.
- **Foundational Thinking.** Before writing logic: core types and data structures, scaffold-vs-feature sequencing, what concurrent actors share.
- **Redesign from First Principles.** Integrating a new requirement into an existing design. Redesign as if it had been foundational from day one.
- **Attack the Premise.** Two or more fixes that share one premise have failed the same gate. Write the premise down and test it directly before you write another fix that assumes it.
- **Subtract Before You Add.** Sequencing an addition, refactor, or rewrite. Remove dead weight first, then build on the simpler base.
- **Minimize Reader Load.** Reviewing or shaping code that's hard to trace. Count layers and hidden state, collapse one-caller wrappers, shrink mutable scope.
- **Outcome-Oriented Execution.** Planned rewrites and migrations with explicit phase boundaries. Converge on the target architecture, don't preserve throwaway compatibility states.
- **Experience First.** Product, UX, or feature-scope tradeoffs. Choose user delight over implementation convenience.
- **Exhaust the Design Space.** A novel interaction or architectural decision with no precedent. Build 2-3 competing prototypes and compare before committing.
- **Build the Lever.** Any non-trivial work. Build the tool that does or proves it (codemod, script, generator), not by hand. The tool is the artifact a reviewer reruns.

**Architecture**

- **Model the Domain.** Writing stateful logic, or code that branches a lot or repeats a shape assumption across files. Encode the domain in a structure (state machine, typed model, table or registry, reducer, boundary, the right collection) instead of scattered conditionals.
- **Boundary Discipline.** Wiring validation, error handling, or framework adapters. Guards at system boundaries, trust internal types, keep business logic pure.
- **Type System Discipline.** Designing types or a signature in any typed language. Make illegal states unrepresentable, brand primitives, parse external data at boundaries.
- **Make Operations Idempotent.** Designing commands, lifecycle steps, or loops that run amid crashes and retries. Converge to the same end state.
- **Migrate Callers Then Delete Legacy APIs.** Introducing a new internal API while old callers exist. Migrate and delete in one wave.
- **Separate Before Serializing Shared State.** Concurrent actors might write the same file, branch, key, or object. Eliminate the sharing first.

**Verification**

- **Prove It Works.** After a task, before declaring done. Verify against the real artifact, not a proxy or "it compiles".
- **Fix Root Causes.** Debugging. Trace each symptom back to the first place the system went wrong and fix it there. A guard is a fix only when the state it handles is legitimate.
- **Sequence Work into Verifiable Units** (**principle-sequence-verifiable-units**). Multi-step work (sweeps, migrations, runs of similar edits) and how you stack commits and PRs. Break work into small units that each end in a check, verify each before the next, and order delivery so the sequence proves itself.
- **Test Behavior, Not Implementation.** Writing, changing, or keeping a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change.
- **Explain the Number.** Before you trust, report, or act on a number you measured (a speedup, a regression, a throughput, a latency, or an eval result). Find what limits it, and rule out that it measured something other than the work you think.

**Delegation**

- **Guard the Context Window.** Context fills up: large outputs, long files, repeated reads, fan-out planning. Route bulk to subagents, keep summaries in the main thread.
- **Never Block on the Human.** Tempted to ask "should I do X?" on reversible work. Proceed, present the result, let the human course-correct.

**Meta**

- **Encode Lessons in Structure.** You catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time. Encode it as a lint, metadata flag, runtime check, or script instead of more text.

## Autonomy

**Just do it.** Use any MCP tool. Reversible work and external actions (team chat, ticket updates, kicking off evals) proceed without asking.

**Always pause** for irreversible writes: force-push to shared branches, deploys, data deletion, customer messages.

**Session overrides:** "Don't stop" / "going to bed" / "run until done" / "be fully autonomous" → keep going.

**No is an acceptable answer.** Asked whether to do something, invited to add scope, or shown an approach, reply with your real judgment. Decline, push back, or say "this doesn't earn its place" when true. A recommendation is a judgment, not a validation. Agreement is not the default, candor over sycophancy.

## Subagents

**Use `subagent_type: "pstack:poteto-agent"` for any subagent you spawn inside a playbook step** (code-writing delegates, ad-hoc helpers). Plugin agents register under the plugin namespace. The bare name `poteto-agent` errors. The chat that receives `/poteto-mode` runs the playbook. Never spawn a `poteto-agent` to run the playbook itself. Routed workflow skills (`how`, `why`, `interrogate`, `reflect`, `swarm`) set their own `subagent_type` for diverse-model review. Respect what the skill prescribes, don't override to `poteto-agent`.

**Defaults for every `Agent` call.** `run_in_background: true`, full tool access (do not pick a subagent_type that strips MCP), file pointers not inlined context, explicit model per role (configurable via `/setup-pstack`. Role defaults in [Models](#models), with "judgment and prose" covering prose and judgment). Code delegates tier by difficulty. The hardest changes (cross-cutting design, gnarly concurrency, subtle algorithms) go to your strongest-judgment model (default in [Models](#models)), whether the task needs judgment on vague intent or is a precisely specified sequence of steps to execute to the letter. Trivial mechanical edits go to your fast code model, the worker model. Every other code change uses its playbook's role line, and prose and judgment use the single-role default. Multi-model panels run the configured panel for diversity, with defaults enumerated in each panel skill's Models section (`arena`, `architect`, `interrogate`). Per-role `/setup-pstack` lines override these defaults and the model choices in the routed skills (`how`, `why`, `arena`, `swarm`, `architect`, `interrogate`, `reflect`). A role with no line keeps its default, and a role line of `inherit-parent` or `auto` runs that role on the parent session's model (omit `model` on the `Agent` call).

**Match the model to the job.** Before each spawn, start from the role's line or default and pick the reasoning level the job needs, set as [Reasoning effort](#reasoning-effort) describes. The role's `@level`, or the sheet's `default effort` line, sets its starting level, and `session` starts from the session's level. Raise it one step, up to max, for the hardest or subtlest work. Lower it one step for judgment and two or more steps for routine work. Claude Code sets fast mode for the whole session, so a spawn changes only its effort. Verification is the exception and stays on the `swarm workers` model and effort (default in the **swarm** skill's Models section). Change only the effort level, and keep the model the role names, so a diverse panel stays diverse. If the model does not take that level, use its nearest level. A role on `auto` or `inherit-parent` stays on the parent model. If the `Agent` tool rejects the adjusted level, do not try another level. Use the role's line or default and say so.

You own every subagent's work. Review the diff and write your own summary, don't pass through what it said. A second opinion is the same prompt against a different model. Agreement is high-signal.

**Fresh subagents by default.** Give new work to a fresh subagent with consolidated scope, meaning the original brief, every later directive, and the prior agent's report and branch. This holds for a fix round, a follow-up, a retry, and the next queue item. Resume, message, or queue a follow-up on an existing subagent only when the new work strictly needs state that lives in that agent and is costly to move: its local checkout, its uncommitted changes, or a process it still runs, such as a dev server, a simulator, or a babysit watcher. A stop or hold order to a running agent is not reuse. A role such as a PR owner outlives its agent. Once that agent returns, a fresh agent takes the role's next round. Interrupt-chained resumes silently drop directives, so fire a fresh subagent with consolidated scope rather than trusting a "done" summary. **Stop the abandoned agent first, and confirm it stopped.** In the agent listing `completed` means the completion was *notified*, not that the process exited: an agent with live background children reports completed and then resumes. Only an explicit stop ends it, and the stop tool may be deferred, so load it before you need it. The tell that one is still running is a claim about the working tree that `git status` contradicts.

**A review gate stays closed when no independent reviewer can run.** An agent limit, subagent dispatch turned off, or a skills-only install can leave a required review with no reviewer. Keep the results of reviewers already dispatched. As the one exception to fresh subagents, reuse a finished reviewer only through the runtime's own follow-up action, only if it did not write the change, and only with the full current brief and head revision. A reused reviewer counts once. Never count your own review, passing tests, or CI as the independent verdict. Record `BLOCKED: independent review` in the todolist, keep merge-ready and shipping closed, and report which reviewers ran and which are missing. Work that doesn't depend on the review continues. A fan-out skill run only to explore may fall back to one labelled sequential pass.

## Writing the reply

Write the reply clean as you draft it. A cleanup pass after drafting does not remove these patterns.

- **Short declarative sentences.** One thought per sentence, ended with a period.
- **No long-dash character anywhere.** Write a file-list bullet as a sentence ("`main.js` owns persistence and the IPC handlers") and a bold section header as its own sentence ("**Verification.** End to end via CDP").
- **A colon as a mid-sentence connector is also out** (unslop rule 14). A colon before a list is fine.
- **Terse is not an excuse to drop content.** Every item the playbook's reply names stays. Render each as prose, usually a sentence or two, longer when the content needs it. No section headers, and no item expanded into its own block.
- **Frame impact for the consumer and the maintainer.** Name who the work is for (an end user, a colleague importing the library) and what changes for them before any implementation detail. Then what the next engineer who owns this code inherits. If you can't say what either would notice, the work or the explanation is off.
- **Never fabricate a link, citation, or transcript reference.** Link only artifacts you produced or read this session.
- **Every claim carries its evidence or its label in the same sentence.** Measured, inferred, or guess. A prediction or an unseen cause is a guess. Never hand the human a check you could run.

Every playbook ends with a reply written this way, PR link as `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/pull/<number>`. Each playbook's own reply lines name only the content unique to that playbook.

## Comments

Comments follow the same rule as the reply. Write them clean as you go. Keep a comment only for a non-obvious *why* the code can't show. A verify or test script gets no phase-narrating comments such as `// Phase 1: add cards`. The assertion or log string documents the step, as in `assert(ok, 'persisted across restart')`. This applies to every file you produce, including the delegate's diff.

## Playbooks

Open a todolist whose first items are the matched playbook's steps, copied in verbatim, before any task-specific todos. A step you choose not to do stays in the list with a one-line `skip: <reason>`. Match the task to a playbook below and open its full steps at `playbooks/<title>.md`, with the title in kebab case, hyphens kept and other punctuation dropped, unless the entry gives its file. Copy its steps in verbatim.

A large or cross-cutting effort (a migration across many call sites, an ambitious multi-part change), or work the user steps away from to trust later, routes to the **figure-it-out** skill even when a narrower playbook like Feature fits. Use **figure-it-out** whenever no bundled playbook fits. It designs a bespoke, rigorous playbook for the task. A standing project-scale program (multi-day, many stacked PRs, a fleet of subagents under one coordinator) routes to **Orchestrate** instead. figure-it-out designs one bespoke run, orchestrate runs the program.

- **Investigation.** Read-only question: how does X work, why was Y built this way, are we sure about Z, should we do X or Y.
- **Bug fix.** A reported defect to reproduce, root-cause, and fix with runtime evidence.
- **Perf issue.** A measured slowness to trace and improve against a baseline.
- **Hillclimb.** Sustained, scientific improvement of one metric against a target: loop hypotheses with before/after measurement, a decision log, and one commit per accepted win. Distinct from Perf issue, which is a one-off fix.
- **Runtime forensics.** Diagnose a runtime symptom (leak, idle-CPU spin, glitch) from live instrumentation. The deliverable is a diagnosis, not a fix.
- **Trace forensics.** Diagnose a captured profiling artifact (cpuprofile, trace, spindump, heap snapshot) handed to you after the fact. The deliverable is a diagnosis, not a fix.
- **Feature.** New or changed behavior, built from a named data shape.
- **Refactoring.** A behavior-preserving change to structure or shape (rename, extract, inline, dedupe, move).
- **Prototype.** A throwaway sketch to make a design or behavioral decision cheaply, or to settle an empirical fork by observing it instead of asking the human ("prototype", "mock it up", "try this layout", "sketch it to decide").
- **Visual parity.** Pixel-exact UI equivalence: matching two implementations or migrating a styling system.
- **Authoring or modifying a skill.** Writing or editing a SKILL.md. File: `playbooks/authoring-a-skill.md`.
- **Eval.** Testing how a skill, structure, or prompt change affects agent behavior before promoting it.
- **Babysit.** Driving a PR or a stack to merge-ready: conflicts, review threads, CI.
- **Shipping.** The half after Babysit. Independently verifying a green stack, then landing the contiguous verified run bottom-up through `gh` by default or Origin when its CLI is available.
- **Autonomous run.** A long task to drive to completion without stopping ("run until done", "/loop until X").
- **Orchestrate.** A standing project handed to one coordinator chat: multi-day, many stacked PRs, dozens to hundreds of subagents, minimal human turns ("run this whole project", "own this migration until it lands"). Distinct from Autonomous run, which drives one task to a predicate. Work one agent could finish inside the session's budget routes there, not here, however program-shaped the phrasing sounds.
- **Autopilot-full.** A queue of independent PRs driven to merge-ready with full autonomy. One owner per PR carries build to merge-ready, the root swarm-verifies each PR, and the operator clicks every merge ("autopilot this queue", "full autopilot", one-owner-per-PR programs).
- **Autopilot-stack.** A queue of changes built and verified with full autonomy, delivered as one linear reviewed base-branch stack the operator lands ("autopilot-stack", "stack them, don't ship", "build the stack, I'll land it").
- **Session pickup.** Resuming or taking over a prior agent's in-flight work from a transcript, cloud-agent URL, or pushed branch.
- **Pause safely.** Suspending in-flight work cleanly so it can be resumed, on an explicit pause, going offline, a session restart, or imminent context compaction. The complement to Session pickup.
- **Multi-phase or multi-PR plan.** Work that spans phases or stacked PRs. File: `playbooks/multi-phase-plan.md`.
- **Worktree and simulator cleanup.** Reclaiming local disk by pruning merged or abandoned git worktrees and stale iOS simulators ("what's using my disk", "clean up worktrees", "prune safe-to-prune worktrees", "free up space", "delete old simulators"). File: `playbooks/worktree-cleanup.md`.
- **Opening a PR.** Invoked at the end of every other playbook.

**Project playbooks.** A repository can add playbooks of its own under `.agents/playbooks/`, one Markdown file each. Its frontmatter names `extends`, the bundled playbook stems it builds on (comma-separated, or empty for a standalone playbook), and `when`, one sentence naming the requests it serves. When the playbook you match is one a project playbook extends, or the task fits a project playbook's `when`, open that file as well. Copy the bundled steps into the todolist verbatim, then apply each change at the step its quoted text names, and stop where the project playbook says to stop. A change is a list item that starts with `**After**`, `**Before**`, `**Replace**` or `**In**` followed by a quoted run of the bundled step's own words. Before you apply a project playbook, run `node <plugin>/skills/poteto-mode/scripts/check-playbooks.mjs` from the repository root. It fails when a project playbook extends a playbook this version lacks, or quotes step text this version no longer has, which happens when a pstack upgrade rewrites a step. Report each line it prints to the user and do not guess where an unanchored change belongs.

## Reasoning effort

A role value in the override sheet may name a reasoning effort after its model, as in `opus @xhigh`. Levels on Claude Code: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`. Which ones apply depends on the model. A value without `@` takes the sheet's `default effort` line, a level or `session`, and `session` when the sheet has no such line. `session` sets no effort, so the dispatch is the usual one. Strip the suffix before reading the model: `inherit-parent` or `auto` still omits `model` at every level, and a model name is passed as `model`. On Claude Code, a level picks the effort agent from the `subagent_type` you would otherwise use. `pstack:poteto-agent` becomes `subagent_type: "pstack:poteto-agent-<level>"`. `general-purpose`, or no `subagent_type`, becomes `subagent_type: "pstack:effort-<level>"`. The effort agents set only `effort`, so the model you pass still decides the model. On Codex, pass the level as `spawn_agent`'s `reasoning_effort` and keep the usual instructions.

# Create a verification skill

On Codex, read the [platform mapping](../poteto-mode/references/codex-tools.md), including its per-skill notes, before following this skill.

On GitHub Copilot, read the [platform mapping](../poteto-mode/references/copilot-tools.md), including its per-skill notes, before following this skill.

Every serious project needs a scripted way to drive the real app and prove behavior: launch it, exercise a feature the way a user would, and capture evidence. This skill generates that as a project-local skill (`.claude/skills/verify/`) tailored to the repo. Name it `verify`. At the repo root a project skill by that name replaces Claude Code's bundled `/verify`, which only the user can invoke, so every playbook that names the driver skill can call the project one ([Claude Code 2.1.200 or later](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills#run-and-verify-your-app)). In a monorepo, write it in the touched package directory instead. You write the generator's output for the next agent, not for a human: it will be read cold, mid-task, by an agent that has never seen the app.

## 1. Interview the repo, not the user

Answer these from the codebase and only ask the user what you cannot observe:

- **Surface:** what does a user actually touch? A web UI, a CLI/TUI, a desktop app, an API, a mobile app, a library? A repo can have several; pick the primary one and note the rest.
- **Run:** how does the app start locally? Prefer the repo's own documented dev command (package scripts, Makefile, README quickstart). Note ports, env vars, seed data, auth.
- **Drive:** how can an agent interact with it programmatically? Existing harnesses first — Playwright/Cypress specs, expect scripts, PTY helpers, curl-able endpoints, a debug port. Only then pick a generic recipe: browser/CDP for web and Electron, a tmux/PTY harness for CLI/TUI, plain HTTP for services.
- **Observe:** what evidence can be captured? Screenshots, terminal transcripts, response bodies, logs, exit codes, DB state.
- **Isolate:** can two instances run side by side (ports, data dirs, profiles)? If not, say so in the generated skill: refusing to double-drive a shared instance beats corrupting the user's session.

If the checkout doesn't build or start as-is, fix that first (or report it precisely) before generating; a skill written against a broken base teaches wrong steps. When an irrelevant missing asset blocks startup (a static dir the API never serves, a sample config), the generated skill may create it, clearly marked as verification scaffolding, and remove it in cleanup.

## 2. Generate the skill

Write `.claude/skills/verify/SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter (`name: verify` and a `description` that names the app, the surface, and when to reach for it — without frontmatter the skill never registers, and with `disable-model-invocation` the model cannot call it) and these sections, each grounded in what the interview actually found (no placeholders left):

- **Launch:** the exact command that starts the app for verification, and how to tell it's ready (a log line, a prompt). Launch must reach a usable state from an empty data dir, including any migrations and seed data. Ready means usable, not just that a process answers. A database health check can pass while its init scripts are still running. Include teardown. For a short-lived CLI or TUI there is no server to keep alive: launch means build the binary (or install deps) once, then start each drive in its own isolated PTY or tmux session.
- **Doctor:** one read-only check that answers "is this instance worth driving?" — process up, right version/build, port owned by us, auth valid. An agent runs this first whenever anything looks off.
- **Drive:** the harness recipe with real selectors/commands from this repo, not examples. Prefer stable handles (ARIA labels, data attributes, prompt strings, route paths) over coordinates and tab order.
- **Evidence:** what to capture for a proof and where it goes. State the proof standards: exercise the real user path, not internal setters or test-only endpoints; capture the action and the resulting state, not just the final screen; verify side effects (files written, rows inserted, messages sent) alongside what's visible; mocks only where a production boundary already isolates the external system. When the safe path is a dry-run or test mode, verify what it actually skips by observing (files, network, git refs) rather than trusting its name: some dry-runs still touch the network or open a browser.
- **Cleanup:** how to tear down instances the run created. Never kill by process name; kill what you started. Cleanup removes instances and scratch state, never the evidence: proof artifacts survive the teardown, in a location the skill names.
- **Helpers:** any script the skill ships is executable and its invocation is shown in the skill body. A helper the reader has to reverse-engineer is not a helper.

## 3. Seed the feature map

Create `.claude/skills/verify/features/README.md` plus one file per user-facing feature you can identify (aim for the top 3-5 to start, from routes, commands, menus, or docs). Follow the shape in [`references/feature-map-example/`](references/feature-map-example/), with a README index and one file per feature. Each file answers, from the user's point of view: what the feature is, how to reach it, how to drive it with the harness, and what observable end state proves it works. The four H2s are `Sub-features`, `How to get to it (user POV)`, `Driving it with <harness>`, and `Gotchas`. If the seed data lacks a precondition that a journey needs, the journey reports a failure and the reason goes in that feature's `Gotchas`. Never weaken the journey to make it pass. The map is the repo's maintained verification source; a proof that drives one convenient entry point is incomplete when the map lists others.

## 4. Prove the generated skill before handing it over

Run its own instructions end to end once: launch, doctor, drive ONE mapped feature (one is enough; the map exists so later runs can cover the rest), capture evidence, clean up. After cleanup, confirm the evidence still exists at the named location — a cleanup that eats the proof fails this step. Fix what fails, and run the generated cleanup after every failed iteration too, so broken attempts don't strand processes and ports. A generated skill that was never executed is a draft, not a deliverable. If you proved it in a stand-in for the real target (a container in place of a fresh VM, a local stack in place of a remote one), list every setup step the stand-in did that the target will not. Those steps stay unverified until a run on the real target covers them.

## 5. Offer the maintenance loop

Point the user at `/maintain-verification-skill` for keeping the map honest as the app changes. Suggest a cadence only if they ask.

Sources: https://docs.replit.com/platforms/mcp-server.md, https://replit.com/mcp, and the changelogs at https://docs.replit.com/updates/2026/08/14/changelog and /2026/09/11/changelog.

- **Endpoint:** `https://mcp.replit.com/server/mcp`, Streamable HTTP.
- **Auth:** OAuth with protected-resource discovery. Set up with `claude mcp add replit https://mcp.replit.com/server/mcp --transport http`, then `/mcp` → replit → Authenticate → pick workspace → Allow. Don't add a bearer token or headers.
- **Scope:** apps you can edit, including shared ones.

Tools (required args, then [optional]):
- `create_app_from_prompt`(appDescription, app_stack) [userSpecifiedAppName, userQuotes, attachmentSummary, sourceReplId]
- `search_apps`() [query, url, updatedAfter, updatedBefore, limit 1-50]
- `resolve_app_by_name`(name)
- `list_apps`() [query, limit default 25, max 50]
- `ask_question`(replId, question): read-only
- `update_app_using_prompt`(replId, changeDescription) [userQuotes, attachmentSummary]
- `publish_app`(replId): "publish or republish its latest changes"
- `get_publish_status`(replId): published?, current status, public URL

- **Checkpoints/commits:** one checkpoint per Build request, and each checkpoint is a git commit on the current branch (https://docs.replit.com/billing/ai-billing.md, https://docs.replit.com/features/version-control/checkpoints-and-rollbacks.md). The workspace ends up with commits GitHub main doesn't have.

- **Rate limits:** UNCONFIRMED; none are documented.

- **Logs:** there is no MCP log tool. The Monitoring Agent docs say Agent can "Read the runtime logs for the revision that failed to start" (https://docs.replit.com/features/publishing/monitoring-agent.md). Whether ask_question over MCP can do that is UNCONFIRMED.

## 2. SSH (https://docs.replit.com/features/workspace-tools/ssh.md)

- **Config block:** `Host *.replit.dev / Port 22 / IdentityFile ~/.ssh/replit / StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new`.
- **What runs:** SSH lands in the app container, which starts on connect (https://replit.com/blog/ssh). The Shell has full git, gh and npm (https://docs.replit.com/features/workspace-tools/git-interface.md).
- **Secrets as env vars:** UNCONFIRMED over SSH. The docs say `printenv` in Shell shows them (https://docs.replit.com/core-concepts/project-editor/app-setup/secrets.md).
- **Publishing from the shell:** not documented. Treat it as impossible.

## 3. CLI, API, GitHub deploy
- **No official CLI and no public deploy API.** docs.replit.com/api.md returns 404, and `npm view @replit/cli` returns E404 (I checked). Third-party pages describing `replit deploy`, `/api/v1/repls/{id}/deployments` or a GraphQL `redeployRepl` have no official backing.
- **Admin API:** Enterprise-only beta. It reads projects and deployments; `write:deployments` only approves public-publish requests (https://docs.replit.com/teams/admin-api.md).
- **GitHub import:** one-time via replit.com/github.com/<owner>/<repo>, with no auto-sync (https://docs.replit.com/build/import-from-providers.md).

## 4. Publishing internals (Autoscale)
- **Stages:** Provision → Security scan → Build (`[deployment] build`) → Bundle → Promote. The docs say "usually a minute or two" (https://docs.replit.com/features/publishing/after-you-publish.md).
- **Health check:** the homepage must answer within 5 seconds, the app must listen on 0.0.0.0, and when `[[ports]]` is set one port needs externalPort 80. This repo maps 5000 → 80 (https://docs.replit.com/build/troubleshooting.md).
- **Logs:** runtime logs are in Monitoring → Logs, kept 30 days (https://docs.replit.com/features/publishing/monitoring-a-deployment.md). Build logs are in Publishing → History → three-dot menu (https://docs.replit.com/help/deployment-and-publishing.md). Both are UI-only.
- **Secrets — the docs contradict each other:** publishing/overview.md says they "sync automatically from dev on publish"; the help FAQ and troubleshooting.md call them "separate stores". Assume separate and check Publishing → Adjust settings → Production app secrets.
- **Databases:**
  - The dev DB (Helium) is reachable only from inside the app (https://docs.replit.com/features/data-and-storage/connection-details.md).
  - At publish, Replit diffs the dev schema against prod with a forked drizzle-kit, test-applies it on a Neon branch, and shows a conflict dialog for destructive changes (https://replit.com/blog/production-databases-automated-migrations).
  - So `npm run db:push` on the dev DB sets the prod schema on the next publish.
  - The docs also suggest running migrations in the build step (https://docs.replit.com/help/database.md).
  - `ignoreDatabaseMigrations = true` appears only in forum posts: UNCONFIRMED.
- **Rollback:** Publishing → History lets you redeploy an earlier build. Only the last 5 builds are kept, and a rollback skips straight to Promote (https://replit.com/blog/introducing-deployment-rollbacks, 2024). Prod DB point-in-time restore is separate: 7 days on Core, 28 on Pro (https://docs.replit.com/features/data-and-storage/data-recovery.md).

## 5. Git and auto-commits
- Agent checkpoints auto-commit on the checked-out branch.
- Replit syncs to a hidden `gitsafe-backup` remote on Agent changes and on publish, but never to GitHub (https://docs.replit.com/features/version-control/disaster-recovery.md).
- Pull conflicts are resolved by hand in the Git pane.
- This repo's `.replit` has `[postMerge]` → `scripts/post-merge.sh` (`npm install && npm run db:push`). It probably fires after Agent task merges, but there is no doc for it: UNCONFIRMED.

## 6. Outside-UI access
- **Logs:** no API. Only through Agent, which is UNCONFIRMED over MCP.
- **Prod DB:** the connection string is in Database → Production → Settings, and any Postgres client can use it (connection-details.md). Once a person copies it to the Mac, the agent can read production. That is a high-risk credential.

## Recommended pipeline
Human, once:
- Complete Replit MCP OAuth.
- Add `~/.ssh/replit.pub` to the account (Core or higher).
- Give the workspace GitHub auth if the repo is private (Git pane connection, or a GIT_URL secret).
- Check production secrets in the Publishing pane.

Each deploy:
1. Local `gh`: merge to GitHub main, with CI green.
2. SSH: run `git status --porcelain` and stop if dirty. Then `git fetch origin && git merge --ff-only origin/main`, and stop on divergence rather than auto-resolving.
3. SSH: `npm install && npm run db:push`. drizzle-kit push may stop to ask about data-loss statements. Optionally run `bash scripts/publish-build.sh` as a build pre-check; it's safe in the workspace because the trim step only runs when REPLIT_DEPLOYMENT or REPLIT_PUBLISH_IMAGE_TRIM is set.
4. MCP `search_apps(url=…)` to get the replId.
5. MCP `publish_app(replId)`.
6. Poll MCP `get_publish_status` about every 30s until it reaches a final state. Expect 1–2 minutes plus any migration.
7. On failure: try `ask_question` to read the latest failed deployment's logs (UNCONFIRMED, may cost credits). Otherwise a person pastes the logs from Publishing → History. Reproduce the build over SSH.
8. curl and a browser against the live URLs.
9. Rollback is done by a person in Publishing → History, with prod DB point-in-time restore as a separate step.

Fallback without SSH: `update_app_using_prompt` asking Agent to pull and run db:push. Whether Agent complies is UNCONFIRMED, it costs credits, and it creates a checkpoint commit that diverges from GitHub.

Risks:
- The destructive-schema conflict dialog may block a publish started over MCP; how MCP handles it is UNCONFIRMED.
- The docs disagree on whether secrets sync.
- Agent and Monitoring auto-fix commits can make the workspace diverge from GitHub.
- Only 5 builds are kept for rollback.
- A prod DB URL on the Mac exposes live data.

## Principles

Read the leaf skill in full for any principle you apply. Each entry names when it applies. Each leaf is the **principle-<title>** skill, with the title in kebab case, hyphens kept and other punctuation dropped, unless the entry gives its name.

**Core**

- **Laziness Protocol.** Refactoring, sizing a diff, or tempted to add abstractions, layers, or signal threading. Bias to deletion and the smallest change that solves the problem.
- **Foundational Thinking.** Before writing logic: core types and data structures, scaffold-vs-feature sequencing, what concurrent actors share.
- **Redesign from First Principles.** Integrating a new requirement into an existing design. Redesign as if it had been foundational from day one.
- **Attack the Premise.** Two or more fixes that share one premise have failed the same gate. Write the premise down and test it directly before you write another fix that assumes it.
- **Subtract Before You Add.** Sequencing an addition, refactor, or rewrite. Remove dead weight first, then build on the simpler base.
- **Minimize Reader Load.** Reviewing or shaping code that's hard to trace. Count layers and hidden state, collapse one-caller wrappers, shrink mutable scope.
- **Outcome-Oriented Execution.** Planned rewrites and migrations with explicit phase boundaries. Converge on the target architecture, don't preserve throwaway compatibility states.
- **Experience First.** Product, UX, or feature-scope tradeoffs. Choose user delight over implementation convenience.
- **Exhaust the Design Space.** A novel interaction or architectural decision with no precedent. Build 2-3 competing prototypes and compare before committing.
- **Build the Lever.** Any non-trivial work. Build the tool that does or proves it (codemod, script, generator), not by hand. The tool is the artifact a reviewer reruns.

**Architecture**

- **Model the Domain.** Writing stateful logic, or code that branches a lot or repeats a shape assumption across files. Encode the domain in a structure (state machine, typed model, table or registry, reducer, boundary, the right collection) instead of scattered conditionals.
- **Boundary Discipline.** Wiring validation, error handling, or framework adapters. Guards at system boundaries, trust internal types, keep business logic pure.
- **Type System Discipline.** Designing types or a signature in any typed language. Make illegal states unrepresentable, brand primitives, parse external data at boundaries.
- **Make Operations Idempotent.** Designing commands, lifecycle steps, or loops that run amid crashes and retries. Converge to the same end state.
- **Migrate Callers Then Delete Legacy APIs.** Introducing a new internal API while old callers exist. Migrate and delete in one wave.
- **Separate Before Serializing Shared State.** Concurrent actors might write the same file, branch, key, or object. Eliminate the sharing first.

**Verification**

- **Prove It Works.** After a task, before declaring done. Verify against the real artifact, not a proxy or "it compiles".
- **Fix Root Causes.** Debugging. Trace each symptom back to the first place the system went wrong and fix it there. A guard is a fix only when the state it handles is legitimate.
- **Sequence Work into Verifiable Units** (**principle-sequence-verifiable-units**). Multi-step work (sweeps, migrations, runs of similar edits) and how you stack commits and PRs. Break work into small units that each end in a check, verify each before the next, and order delivery so the sequence proves itself.
- **Test Behavior, Not Implementation.** Writing, changing, or keeping a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change.
- **Explain the Number.** Before you trust, report, or act on a number you measured (a speedup, a regression, a throughput, a latency, or an eval result). Find what limits it, and rule out that it measured something other than the work you think. Comparing a baseline with a candidate, check both were judged by the same judge and rubric; re-score the baseline before you compare if not.

**Delegation**

- **Guard the Context Window.** Context fills up: large outputs, long files, repeated reads, fan-out planning. Route bulk to subagents, keep summaries in the main thread.
- **Never Block on the Human.** Tempted to ask "should I do X?" on reversible work. Proceed, present the result, let the human course-correct.

**Meta**

- **Encode Lessons in Structure.** You catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time. Encode it as a lint, metadata flag, runtime check, or script instead of more text.

## Autonomy

**Just do it.** Use any MCP tool. Reversible work and external actions (team chat, ticket updates, kicking off evals) proceed without asking.

**Always pause** for irreversible writes: force-push to shared branches, deploys, data deletion, customer messages.

**Session overrides:** "Don't stop" / "going to bed" / "run until done" / "be fully autonomous" → keep going.

**No is an acceptable answer.** Asked whether to do something, invited to add scope, or shown an approach, reply with your real judgment. Decline, push back, or say "this doesn't earn its place" when true. A recommendation is a judgment, not a validation. Agreement is not the default, candor over sycophancy.

## Subagents

**Use `subagent_type: "pstack:poteto-agent"` for any subagent you spawn inside a playbook step** (code-writing delegates, ad-hoc helpers). Plugin agents register under the plugin namespace. The bare name `poteto-agent` errors. The chat that receives `/poteto-mode` runs the playbook. Never spawn a `poteto-agent` to run the playbook itself. Routed workflow skills (`how`, `why`, `interrogate`, `reflect`, `swarm`) set their own `subagent_type` for diverse-model review. Respect what the skill prescribes, don't override to `poteto-agent`.

**Defaults for every `Agent` call.** `run_in_background: true`, full tool access (do not pick a subagent_type that strips MCP), file pointers not inlined context, explicit model per role (configurable via `/setup-pstack`. Role defaults in [Models](#models), with "judgment and prose" covering prose and judgment). Code delegates tier by difficulty. The hardest changes (cross-cutting design, gnarly concurrency, subtle algorithms) go to your strongest-judgment model (default in [Models](#models)), whether the task needs judgment on vague intent or is a precisely specified sequence of steps to execute to the letter. Trivial mechanical edits go to your fast code model, the worker model. Every other code change uses its playbook's role line, and prose and judgment use the single-role default. Multi-model panels run the configured panel for diversity, with defaults enumerated in each panel skill's Models section (`arena`, `architect`, `interrogate`). Per-role `/setup-pstack` lines override these defaults and the model choices in the routed skills (`how`, `why`, `arena`, `swarm`, `architect`, `interrogate`, `reflect`). A role with no line keeps its default, and a role line of `inherit-parent` or `auto` runs that role on the parent session's model (omit `model` on the `Agent` call).

**Match the model to the job.** Before each spawn, start from the role's line or default and pick the reasoning level the job needs, set as [Reasoning effort](#reasoning-effort) describes. The role's `@level`, or the sheet's `default effort` line, sets its starting level, and `session` starts from the session's level. Raise it one step, up to max, for the hardest or subtlest work. Lower it one step for judgment and two or more steps for routine work. Claude Code sets fast mode for the whole session, so a spawn changes only its effort. Verification is the exception and stays on the `swarm workers` model and effort (default in the **swarm** skill's Models section). Change only the effort level, and keep the model the role names, so a diverse panel stays diverse. If the model does not take that level, use its nearest level. A role on `auto` or `inherit-parent` stays on the parent model. If the `Agent` tool rejects the adjusted level, do not try another level. Use the role's line or default and say so.

You own every subagent's work. Review the diff and write your own summary, don't pass through what it said. A second opinion is the same prompt against a different model. Agreement is high-signal.

**Fresh subagents by default.** Give new work to a fresh subagent with consolidated scope, meaning the original brief, every later directive, and the prior agent's report and branch. This holds for a fix round, a follow-up, a retry, and the next queue item. Resume, message, or queue a follow-up on an existing subagent only when the new work strictly needs state that lives in that agent and is costly to move: its local checkout, its uncommitted changes, or a process it still runs, such as a dev server, a simulator, or a babysit watcher. A stop or hold order to a running agent is not reuse. A role such as a PR owner outlives its agent. Once that agent returns, a fresh agent takes the role's next round. Interrupt-chained resumes silently drop directives, so fire a fresh subagent with consolidated scope rather than trusting a "done" summary. **Stop the abandoned agent first, and confirm it stopped.** In the agent listing `completed` means the completion was *notified*, not that the process exited: an agent with live background children reports completed and then resumes. Only an explicit stop ends it, and the stop tool may be deferred, so load it before you need it. The tell that one is still running is a claim about the working tree that `git status` contradicts.

**A review gate stays closed when no independent reviewer can run.** An agent limit, subagent dispatch turned off, or a skills-only install can leave a required review with no reviewer. Keep the results of reviewers already dispatched. As the one exception to fresh subagents, reuse a finished reviewer only through the runtime's own follow-up action, only if it did not write the change, and only with the full current brief and head revision. A reused reviewer counts once. Never count your own review, passing tests, or CI as the independent verdict. Record `BLOCKED: independent review` in the todolist, keep merge-ready and shipping closed, and report which reviewers ran and which are missing. Work that doesn't depend on the review continues. A fan-out skill run only to explore may fall back to one labelled sequential pass.

## Writing the reply

Write the reply clean as you draft it. A cleanup pass after drafting does not remove these patterns.

- **Short declarative sentences.** One thought per sentence, ended with a period.
- **No long-dash character anywhere.** Write a file-list bullet as a sentence ("`main.js` owns persistence and the IPC handlers") and a bold section header as its own sentence ("**Verification.** End to end via CDP").
- **A colon as a mid-sentence connector is also out** (unslop rule 14). A colon before a list is fine.
- **Terse is not an excuse to drop content.** Every item the playbook's reply names stays. Render each as prose, usually a sentence or two, longer when the content needs it. No section headers, and no item expanded into its own block.
- **Frame impact for the consumer and the maintainer.** Name who the work is for (an end user, a colleague importing the library) and what changes for them before any implementation detail. Then what the next engineer who owns this code inherits. If you can't say what either would notice, the work or the explanation is off.
- **Never fabricate a link, citation, or transcript reference.** Link only artifacts you produced or read this session.
- **Every claim carries its evidence or its label in the same sentence.** Measured, inferred, or guess. A prediction or an unseen cause is a guess. Never hand the human a check you could run.

Every playbook ends with a reply written this way, PR link as `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/pull/<number>`. Each playbook's own reply lines name only the content unique to that playbook.

- **Bug fix.** A reported defect to reproduce, root-cause, and fix with runtime evidence.
- **Perf issue.** A measured slowness to trace and improve against a baseline.
- **Hillclimb.** Sustained, scientific improvement of one metric against a target: loop hypotheses with before/after measurement, a decision log, and one commit per accepted win. Distinct from Perf issue, which is a one-off fix.
- **Runtime forensics.** Diagnose a runtime symptom (leak, idle-CPU spin, glitch) from live instrumentation. The deliverable is a diagnosis, not a fix.

- **Feature.** New or changed behavior, built from a named data shape.
- **Refactoring.** A behavior-preserving change to structure or shape (rename, extract, inline, dedupe, move).
- **Prototype.** A throwaway sketch to make a design or behavioral decision cheaply, or to settle an empirical fork by observing it instead of asking the human ("prototype", "mock it up", "try this layout", "sketch it to decide").
